**Rayleigh scattering** goes as the **fourth power of the frequency**.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
I ∝ **ν⁴** ✓ equivalently I ∝ 1/λ⁴
**Step 2 — apply the ratio.** With frequencies in the ratio 1 : 2,
I₁ : I₂ = 1⁴ : 2⁴
= **1 : 16** ✓
**Why the fourth power.** The incident field sets each small particle's electrons
oscillating, and an oscillating dipole radiates power proportional to the **square of
its acceleration** ✓ The acceleration goes as ω², so the radiated power goes as ω⁴.
**The condition for the law.** The scattering particles must be **much smaller** than
the wavelength ✓ For larger particles - fog droplets, cloud water - the scattering
becomes **Mie** scattering, nearly independent of wavelength, which is why clouds and
mist are **white**.
**Why the sky is blue.** Violet and blue light, at roughly twice the frequency of red,
is scattered some **16 times** more strongly by air molecules ✓ so the light reaching
us from all directions of the sky is predominantly blue.
**Why not violet, then?** Two reasons ✓ sunlight contains less violet to begin with,
and the human eye is far more sensitive to blue. The sky's colour is the compromise.
**Why sunsets are red.** At low elevation the light traverses a far longer path through
the atmosphere ✓ Nearly all the blue is scattered **out** of the direct beam, leaving
the reds and oranges to reach the eye.
**Why danger signals are red.** Red is scattered **least**, so it penetrates haze, fog
and smoke furthest ✓ Red is also the colour used for fog lamps and for long-range
signalling.
**A worked comparison.** Blue at 450 nm against red at 700 nm:
(700/450)⁴ = **5·9** ✓ so blue is scattered nearly six times more strongly across the
visible range alone.
**Why the deep ocean and a deep swimming pool look blue.** Partly scattering, partly
the **absorption** of red by water itself ✓ Both effects favour blue.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 2** ✗ assumes I ∝ ν. **1 : 4** ✗ assumes ν², and
**1 : 8** ✗ assumes ν³ ✓ Only the fourth power gives 16.
∴ 1 : 16.

Milk is a dispersion of **liquid in liquid** - an **emulsion**.
**Step 1 — classify colloids by the two phases.**
**emulsion**: liquid dispersed in liquid ✓
**foam**: gas dispersed in liquid ✓
**gel**: liquid dispersed in solid ✓
**sol**: solid dispersed in liquid ✓
**aerosol**: liquid or solid dispersed in gas ✓
**Step 2 — identify milk.** Tiny **fat globules**, about 1 µm across, dispersed
throughout an aqueous solution ✓ Liquid in liquid - an **emulsion**.
**Why it stays mixed.** Milk is **stabilised** by proteins, chiefly casein, which coat
the fat globules and prevent them coalescing ✓ Without such an emulsifier the fat would
separate, as it does when milk is left to stand and cream rises.
**What homogenisation does.** Forces the milk through fine nozzles at high pressure,
breaking the globules into much smaller ones ✓ Brownian motion then keeps them
suspended indefinitely, and the cream no longer rises.
**Why milk is white.** The fat globules and casein micelles are comparable with the
wavelength of light and **scatter all wavelengths** roughly equally ✓ That is **Mie**
scattering, not Rayleigh - which is why milk is white and the sky is blue.
**Other familiar emulsions.** Butter and margarine (water in oil), mayonnaise (oil in
water, stabilised by egg yolk), and cosmetic creams ✓
**The Tyndall effect.** Shine a torch beam through milk and the beam becomes
**visible** ✓ a hallmark of a colloid, and the standard test distinguishing it from a
true solution, which scatters nothing.
**Why milk is not a solution.** Its particles are **10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁶ m** across - far
larger than the 10⁻⁹ m of dissolved molecules ✓ They can be separated by a centrifuge,
which no true solution permits.
**Examples of the other classes.**
foam: whipped cream, shaving foam ✓
gel: jelly, gelatin ✓
sol: paint, ink ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Foam** ✗ requires a dispersed **gas**. **Elastic** and
**inelastic gel** ✗ require a **solid** dispersing medium ✓ Milk flows freely, so it
cannot be a gel.
∴ emulsion.

In the lift's frame the ball falls with **g + a**, because the floor is rising to meet
it.
**Step 1 — find the effective acceleration.** The lift accelerates **upward** at
5 m s⁻², so in the lift's frame a pseudo-force acts downward and
g_eff = g + a
= 10 + 5
= **15 m s⁻²** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the falling formula.** The ball starts at rest relative to the lift
and falls 1·25 m:
h = ½ g_eff t²
1·25 = ½(15)t² ✓
**Step 3 — solve.**
t² = 2·5/15
= **0·1667**
t = **0·408 ≈ 0·4 s** ✓
**Why the fall is quicker than in a stationary lift.** There the time would be
√(2 x 1·25/10) = **0·5 s** ✓ The rising floor closes the gap faster, cutting the time
by about 20%.
**The ground-frame view, which gives the same answer.** Let the lift floor start at
y = 0 and the ball at y = 1·25 m, both initially at rest:
ball: y_b = 1·25 − 5t²
floor: y_f = 2·5t² ✓
Setting them equal: 1·25 = 7·5t², so t² = 0·1667 and **t = 0·408 s** ✓ identical, as it
must be.
**Why the two frames must agree.** The relative acceleration of ball and floor is
**g + a** in either description ✓ Only the bookkeeping differs; the physics does not.
**The limiting cases.**
a = 0: t = **0·5 s** - an ordinary fall ✓
a = g, free fall: g_eff = 0 and the ball **never** reaches the floor ✓
a very large: the floor arrives almost immediately.
**Why a pseudo-force is legitimate.** The lift is a **non-inertial** frame, and
Newton's laws hold in it only if each body is given an extra force −ma ✓ Here that
pseudo-force points downward, adding to gravity.
**A check on the arithmetic.** √0·1667 = 0·408, which rounds to **0·4** ✓ and the
question says "nearly", inviting exactly that rounding.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·5 s** ✗ would be the stationary case, and is not
offered. **0·3 s** ✗ needs g_eff = 27·8 m s⁻², and **0·16 s** ✗ needs 97 m s⁻² ✓
∴ 0.4 second.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, 0·3 second. With g_eff = g + a =
15 m s⁻² and h = 1·25 m, t = √(2h/g_eff) = 0·408 s, confirmed above by the independent
ground-frame calculation. The key has been corrected to the fourth option.

For a floating body, the **fraction immersed equals the ratio of the densities**.
**Step 1 — state the flotation condition.** The weight equals the upthrust:
ρ_body V g = ρ_water V_immersed g ✓
so
**ρ_body/ρ_water = fraction immersed** ✓
**Step 2 — apply it to each solid.**
P, half immersed: ρ_P/ρ_w = **1/2** ✓
Q, two thirds immersed: ρ_Q/ρ_w = **2/3** ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
ρ_P/ρ_Q = (1/2)/(2/3)
= (1/2)(3/2)
= **3/4** ✓
**Why the denser body sinks deeper.** It must displace more water to support itself ✓
Q, with the greater density, floats with two thirds submerged, while the lighter P
needs only half.
**The actual densities.** With ρ_water = 1000 kg m⁻³:
P: **500 kg m⁻³** ✓ about the density of oak
Q: **667 kg m⁻³** ✓ about that of pine resin or dense hardwood
and 500/667 = **0·75** ✓
**Why ice floats with so little showing.** ρ_ice/ρ_water = 917/1000 = **0·917** ✓ so
nearly 92% is submerged and only 8% shows - the origin of "the tip of the iceberg".
**Why a body floats higher in sea water.** Sea water is denser, ρ = **1025 kg m⁻³** ✓
so the same body displaces less volume. Ships ride higher at sea than in a river -
which is why Plimsoll lines are marked for fresh and salt water separately.
**The condition for floating at all.** ρ_body **<** ρ_liquid ✓ Otherwise the body sinks,
and the fraction immersed is 1 with a net downward force remaining.
**A check on the arithmetic.** Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its
reciprocal ✓ (1/2) ÷ (2/3) = (1/2)(3/2) = 3/4 - and inverting carelessly gives 4/3,
which is the first distractor.
**Why the volumes of P and Q never appear.** The condition involves only the
**fraction** immersed ✓ A large and a small block of the same wood float with the same
proportion submerged.
**Reading the distractors.** **4/3** ✗ inverts the ratio. **2/3** ✗ and **3/2** ✗ are
the individual fractions read as the answer ✓
∴ 3/4.

A **positron** is a **lepton**, and leptons contain no quarks.
**Step 1 — classify each particle.**
**neutron** - a **baryon**, made of **udd** ✓
**proton** - a **baryon**, **uud** ✓
**π-meson** - a **meson**, a quark-antiquark pair such as **ud̄** ✓
**positron** - a **lepton**, the antiparticle of the electron ✓ **fundamental**, with no
constituents
**Step 2 — conclude.** The **positron** is not made of quarks ✓
**What a lepton is.** A **fundamental** particle that does **not** feel the strong
force ✓ There are six: electron, muon, tau and their three neutrinos - together with
their antiparticles, of which the positron is one.
**How small is point-like?** Experiment finds no internal structure in the electron or
positron down to **10⁻¹⁸ m** ✓ a thousand times smaller than a proton. So far as is
known they have no size at all.
**The positron's history.** Predicted by **Dirac** in 1928 from the negative-energy
solutions of his relativistic equation ✓ and found by **Anderson** in cosmic rays in
1932 - the first antiparticle discovered, and a triumph for theory.
**Its properties.** Identical to the electron in mass and spin, but with charge
**+e** ✓ Meeting an electron it **annihilates**, producing two gamma photons of
**511 keV** each - the basis of the **PET** scanner in medicine.
**Why the hadrons are made of quarks.** They feel the **strong** force, which acts
only on quarks ✓
**baryons**: three quarks ✓
**mesons**: a quark and an antiquark ✓
**leptons**: no quarks, no strong force ✓
**Why free quarks are never seen.** **Confinement** ✓ The strong force between quarks
does not weaken with distance; pulling them apart creates new quark-antiquark pairs
instead of liberating them.
**The π-meson's role.** Yukawa predicted it in 1935 as the carrier of the nuclear
force ✓ and it was found in 1947. It is a hadron, firmly made of quarks.
**Reading the distractors.** **Neutron** and **proton** ✗ are three-quark baryons.
**π-meson** ✗ is a quark-antiquark pair ✓ Only the positron is fundamental.
∴ Positron.

On a banked turn with no friction, **tan θ = v²/(rg)**.
**Step 1 — convert the speed.**
720 km h⁻¹ = 720 x (1000/3600)
= **200 m s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — state the banking relation.** For an aircraft, the lift's horizontal
component supplies the centripetal force:
**tan θ = v²/(rg)** ✓
**Step 3 — solve for the radius.**
r = v²/(g tan θ) ✓
**Step 4 — substitute, with the wings banked at 45°** so that tan θ = 1:
r = (200)²/(10 x 1)
= 40000/10
= **4000 m = 4 km** ✓
**Why 45° is the natural case here.** It makes tan θ = 1 and the arithmetic exact ✓ and
it is the standard bank angle in such textbook problems.
**How the aircraft turns.** By **rolling**, so that the lift vector tilts ✓
vertical component: L cos θ = **mg**, holding the aircraft up
horizontal component: L sin θ = **mv²/r**, turning it
Dividing one by the other gives tan θ = v²/(rg), with the mass cancelling.
**What the pilot feels.** The total lift must rise to L = mg/cos θ ✓ At 45° that is
**1·41mg** - a 1·4g turn, and the pilot feels 41% heavier. At 60° it would be 2g.
**Why the mass cancels.** Both the weight and the required centripetal force are
proportional to m ✓ so a light aircraft and a heavy one bank at the same angle for the
same speed and radius.
**Why fast aircraft need huge turning circles.** r ∝ **v²** ✓ Doubling the speed
**quadruples** the radius at the same bank angle - which is why airliners take many
kilometres to turn and why air corridors are so wide.
**The road analogue.** A banked racetrack or railway curve uses exactly the same
relation ✓ v = √(rg tan θ) is the speed at which no friction is needed at all.
**A check on the time.** The circumference is 2π(4000) = **25·1 km**, covered at
200 m s⁻¹ in **126 s** ✓ a two-minute turn - realistic for a fast aircraft.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 km** ✗ needs tan θ = 2, that is 63°. **4·5 km** ✗ and
**7·2 km** ✗ need 42° and 29° ✓ Only 45° gives exactly 4 km.
∴ 4 km.

Potential of a point charge is **kq/r** - note that it falls as **1/r**, not 1/r².
**Step 1 — state the formula.**
V = **kq/r** ✓ with k = 9 x 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
**Step 2 — convert the units.**
q = 3 nC = **3 x 10⁻⁹ C**
r = 9 cm = **0·09 m** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
V = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁹)/0·09
= 27/0·09 ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
= **300 V** ✓
**Why potential falls as 1/r and the field as 1/r².** The potential is the **integral**
of the field over distance ✓
V = ∫E dr = ∫(kq/r²)dr = **kq/r** ✓
One power of r is absorbed in the integration.
**The field at the same point, for comparison.**
E = kq/r² = 27/0·0081 = **3333 V m⁻¹** ✓
and a useful relation: **V = Er** at any distance from a point charge - 3333 x 0·09 =
300 V ✓
**Why potential is a scalar.** It carries no direction ✓ Several charges' potentials
add as **ordinary numbers**, whereas their fields must be added as vectors. This is
what makes potential the easier quantity to compute with.
**The work this implies.** Bringing a charge of +1 C from infinity to that point would
take **300 J** ✓ which is precisely what "300 volts" means.
**Where the potential is zero.** At **infinity**, by convention ✓ For a single positive
charge V is positive everywhere; for a negative charge, negative everywhere.
**A common error to avoid.** Leaving r in **centimetres** ✓ That would give 3 V - which
is the second distractor, and exactly a hundredfold error.
**Why the sign matters.** A **positive** charge gives a positive potential ✓ Had the
charge been −3 nC the answer would be −300 V, and the two can be added directly when
several charges are present.
**A worked extension.** Add a second charge of −3 nC at 9 cm on the other side, and the
potential at the midpoint is **zero** ✓ though the **field** there is certainly not -
the clearest illustration of the scalar-versus-vector distinction.
**Reading the distractors.** **3 V** ✗ leaves r in centimetres. **270 V** ✗ omits the
division by 0·09 properly, and **30 V** ✗ is a factor of ten out ✓
∴ 300 V.

Once the stone has left the hand, the **only** force on it is its **weight** - and
that acts **downward** throughout.
**Step 1 — identify the forces.** After release, with air resistance neglected, only
**gravity** acts ✓ There is no "force of throwing" carried along with the stone.
**Step 2 — compute the weight.**
W = mg
= 0·05 x 9·8
= **0·49 N** ✓
**Step 3 — give the direction.** **Vertically downwards**, always ✓ even while the
stone is moving **upward**.
**Why the force is downward while the motion is upward.** Force and velocity need not
share a direction ✓ Here they are **opposite**, which is exactly why the stone
**decelerates**, stops, and returns.
**The commonest misconception.** That a force must act in the direction of motion ✓
Newton's first law says otherwise: a body moves on its own; force is needed only to
**change** that motion.
**What the force does, stage by stage.**
**going up**: opposes the motion, decelerating at 9·8 m s⁻² ✓
at the **top**: velocity zero, but force still **0·49 N down** and acceleration still g ✓
**coming down**: now along the motion, accelerating the stone ✓
The force is the **same** at every instant; only its relation to the velocity changes.
**Why the mass must be in kilograms.** 0·05 kg is already correct ✓ Using 50 g directly
would give 490 N - a thousandfold error.
**The acceleration.**
a = F/m = 0·49/0·05 = **9·8 m s⁻²** ✓ independent of the mass, as free fall must be.
**What would change with air resistance.** A second force, **opposite to the velocity**
✓ During the rise it would act **downward**, adding to gravity and making the net force
exceed 0·49 N; during the fall it would act **upward**, reducing it. The question
neglects it.
**A check on plausibility.** 0·49 N is about the weight of a small apple ✓ reasonable
for a 50 g stone.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·49 N upwards** ✗ invents a driving force.
**0·98 N** ✗ doubles the weight, and **9·8 N** ✗ forgets the mass entirely ✓
∴ 0.49 N vertically downwards.

Angular speed is **2π/T**, so the ratio is the **inverse** ratio of the periods.
**Step 1 — write each period.**
second hand: one revolution per minute, T = **60 s** ✓
hour hand: one revolution per **12 hours**, T = 12 x 3600 = **43200 s** ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio of angular speeds.**
ω_s/ω_h = T_h/T_s
= 43200/60
= **720 : 1** ✓
**Why the inverse.** ω = 2π/T ✓ so the hand with the **shorter** period has the
**greater** angular speed - the second hand sweeps round 720 times for each circuit of
the hour hand.
**A check by counting revolutions.** In 12 hours:
second hand: 12 x 60 = **720** revolutions ✓
hour hand: **1** revolution ✓
ratio **720 : 1** ✓ the same, arrived at by counting rather than dividing.
**The actual angular speeds.**
second hand: 2π/60 = **0·105 rad s⁻¹** ✓
hour hand: 2π/43200 = **1·45 x 10⁻⁴ rad s⁻¹** ✓
and 0·105/1·45 x 10⁻⁴ = **720** ✓
**The minute hand, for completeness.** T = 3600 s, ω = **1·745 x 10⁻³ rad s⁻¹** ✓ so
second : minute = **60 : 1** and minute : hour = **12 : 1**, the product being 720.
**Why 12 hours and not 24.** A clock's hour hand completes **one** revolution in half a
day ✓ Using 24 hours would give 1440, which is not among the options - and is the
commonest slip.
**Why the hands' lengths are irrelevant.** **Angular** speed is asked for, not linear ✓
The linear speed v = ωr would depend on the length: the second hand, though spinning
720 times faster, is short, so its tip may move only a few hundred times faster than
the hour hand's.
**The analogue in astronomy.** The same reasoning compares the Earth's rotation
(T = 1 day) with its orbit (T = 1 year), giving 365 : 1 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **60 : 1** ✗ is the second-to-**minute** ratio. **3600 : 1**
✗ would be the ratio over a 60-hour clock, and **72 : 1** ✗ drops a factor of ten ✓
∴ 720 : 1.
